subtopicTitle: Smart pointers — unique_ptr (sole ownership), shared_ptr (shared ownership, ref count), weak_ptr (break cycles)

cards.front: What fundamental problem in C++ memory management do smart pointers primarily address?
cards.back: Smart pointers automate memory deallocation, preventing memory leaks and dangling pointers by implementing the Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) principle, ensuring resources are released when they go out of scope.

cards.front: Describe the ownership model of `std::unique_ptr` and explain why it cannot be copied.
cards.back: `std::unique_ptr` enforces *sole ownership*. Only one `unique_ptr` can point to a specific resource at any given time. Copying would violate this, as it would create two `unique_ptr`s owning the same resource, leading to double deletion. It can only be *moved*.

cards.front: How can you transfer ownership of a dynamically allocated object from one `std::unique_ptr` to another? Provide a minimal code snippet.
cards.back:
Ownership is transferred using `std::move`.
```cpp
std::unique_ptr<int> ptr1 = std::make_unique<int>(10);
std::unique_ptr<int> ptr2 = std::move(ptr1); // ptr1 is now null, ptr2 owns the int
// *ptr1 would be undefined behavior
std::cout << *ptr2 << std::endl; // Outputs 10
```

cards.front: Explain the ownership model of `std::shared_ptr` and how it determines when the managed object should be deallocated.
cards.back: `std::shared_ptr` implements *shared ownership*. Multiple `shared_ptr` instances can co-own the same resource. It uses an internal *reference count*. The managed object is deallocated only when the last `shared_ptr` instance owning it is destroyed or reset, causing the reference count to drop to zero.

cards.front: Why is `std::make_shared<T>(args...)` generally preferred over `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T(args...))` for creating `std::shared_ptr` instances?
cards.back: `std::make_shared` performs a single memory allocation for both the object `T` and the control block (which contains the reference counts and deleter). Using `new T(...)` followed by the constructor requires two separate allocations, which is less efficient and can be less exception-safe if a raw `new` allocation fails before the `shared_ptr` constructor is called.

cards.front: What specific problem does `std::weak_ptr` solve when working with `std::shared_ptr`, and how does it prevent this issue?
cards.back: `std::weak_ptr` solves the problem of *circular references* between `std::shared_ptr` objects. If two objects hold `shared_ptr`s to each other, their reference counts will never drop to zero, leading to a memory leak. `std::weak_ptr` provides *non-owning observation*; it points to an object managed by a `shared_ptr` without incrementing its reference count, thus allowing the cycle to be broken and objects to be deallocated correctly.
